title: Rishabh Garg, Tesla Optimus — Challenges in High Performance Robotics Systems

summary: Rishabh Garg presents a systematic walkthrough of software-hardware integration challenges in robotics, using a toy system architecture with actuators, CPU, GPU, sensors, and CAN bus communication. The central question is root cause analysis: when a robot misbehaves, is the problem in the RL policy or the software system? He begins with a simple synchronous code loop expecting 2ms cycle times, but discovers 1ms gaps caused by CAN bus saturation—10 messages of 100 bits each at 1 Mbps consume 1ms, comparable to the loop time itself. The first solution accepts the delay, but for high performance, he introduces multithreading with pipelined TX, policy, and RX stages, staggering iterations to achieve faster loop times. This introduces new problems: actuator stuttering and abnormal motor behavior that appear policy-related but aren't. Using external CAN transceivers and candump utilities, he captures timestamped bus data revealing jitter—messages arriving with irregular spacing. Cycle time plots identify TX-side desynchronization where policy runtime variability causes missed send windows and queued messages sent in bursts. RX-side desynchronization causes policies to operate on stale data, producing skip-and-catch-up behavior. Solutions include kernel synchronization primitives or timing padding. Logging pitfalls include disk writes freezing a Raspberry Pi for 30ms and microcontroller logging cascading packet drops. The talk concludes with priority inversion: boosting process priorities so high that the kernel is blocked prevents data reception, causing multi-second system dropouts. The fix requires understanding the full pipeline, setting correct priorities, and ensuring the system works cohesively. Garg recaps the five key areas: pipelining to reduce cycle time, synchronization to avoid jitter, logging strategies that don't block the system, and priority inversion management to avoid starvation.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Root Cause Dilemma
sections.summary: Garg introduces the core problem: when robots misbehave, it's unclear whether the RL policy or the software system is at fault. He proposes building a toy robotics system to explore instances where issues look policy-related but are actually software problems.

sections.title: Toy System Architecture and CAN Bus
sections.summary: Describes a general robot architecture with actuators, CPU, hybrid accelerator, and sensors connected via CAN bus. CAN is chosen for being open source, cheap, and having adequate data rate. A simple synchronous code loop is introduced with an expected 2ms policy cycle time.

sections.title: CAN Bus Saturation and Loop Gaps
sections.summary: Deployment reveals 1ms gaps in the loop. Analysis shows 10 messages of 100 bits each at 1 Mbps take 1ms total, saturating the bus and explaining the gap. The initial solution is to accept the delay, but for high performance, multithreading and pipelining are proposed.

sections.title: Pipelined Multithreaded Design
sections.summary: The loop is broken into TX, policy, and RX components running in separate threads. By staggering iterations—feeding data to policy, starting next RX before policy concludes, and transmitting previous policy output—parallelized communication achieves faster loop times.

sections.title: New Problems: Stuttering and Bus Diagnostics
sections.summary: The pipelined system exhibits actuator stuttering and weird motions. Using external CAN transceivers and candump on a host laptop, timestamped bus data reveals jitter: messages with irregular spacing, including 4ms gaps followed by near-zero gaps, causing actuators to catch up or follow two commands simultaneously.

sections.title: Cycle Time Plots and Desynchronization Analysis
sections.summary: Cycle time plots reveal TX-side desynchronization where policy runtime variability causes missed send windows and queued messages sent in bursts. RX-side desynchronization causes policies to operate on stale data, producing skip-and-catch-up motor behavior. Solutions include kernel synchronization primitives or timing padding.

sections.title: Logging Pitfalls
sections.summary: Logging can severely impact performance: disk writes froze a Raspberry Pi for 30ms, necessitating a dedicated logging CPU. On microcontrollers, logging a dropped packet can take long enough to cause the next drop, creating a cascade of drops with no data on the bus.

sections.title: Priority Inversion and Conclusion
sections.summary: Priority inversion occurs when robotics engineers boost process priorities so high they block the kernel, which prevents the very data reception they need—the system can drop out for seconds at a time. The fix requires understanding the full pipeline, setting correct priorities, and ensuring the system works cohesively. Garg recaps the talk: pipelining to reduce cycle time, synchronization to avoid hard-to-diagnose jitter, logging strategies that don't block the system, and priority inversion management to avoid starvation. These fundamentals underpin high-performance robotic system design.
